analysis.one_liner: Doubles the federal tax deduction for state and local taxes for married couples to $20,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a Senate committee referral and died with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law capped the federal deduction for state and local taxes (SALT) at $10,000 per household. This bill would have raised the cap to $20,000 for married couples filing jointly, backdated to 2018, through 2025. That deduction matters most to households with large property and income tax bills — overwhelmingly higher-income households in high-tax states like New York, New Jersey, and California.
analysis.who_benefits: Married homeowners and high earners in states with high property and income taxes. Raising the SALT cap is one of the most regressive tax cuts available: the benefits flow heavily to households earning well into six figures, with a large share going to the top few percent of earners.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy joint filers in high-tax states

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the state and local tax deduction cap from $10,000 to $20,000 for joint filers, for tax years 2018 through 2025.
Applies retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2018, so filers could amend returns to claim it for years already filed.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers overall, and ultimately federal programs, since the lost revenue would be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. Lower-income households get nothing from the change because they generally do not itemize deductions or pay enough state and local tax to hit the cap.

drawbacks.text: The tax cut is heavily skewed toward high earners: only households with state and local tax bills above $10,000 — overwhelmingly upper-income homeowners in high-tax states — would benefit at all.
Reducing federal revenue by billions would either deepen deficits or shift the cost onto other taxpayers, while doing nothing for the majority of households who take the standard deduction.
The cap is a backstop against federal tax policy subsidizing state and local taxes; a higher cap would encourage higher state and local spending by making it partly federally deductible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households that would qualify — largely affluent joint filers in states like New York and New Jersey — the relief is real, potentially thousands of dollars per year. But the costs are spread across everyone and the benefits are concentrated at the top, making this one of the least broadly shared tax cuts available. Its retroactivity also raises fairness questions, since it would deliver refunds for taxes already paid.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, gained zero cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Susan Collins introduced the bill on October 31, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No further action was taken: the bill never left the Finance Committee and never received a vote in either chamber.
It attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime.
The bill would have raised the state and local tax deduction cap to $20,000 for joint filers, for tax years 2018 through 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal treasury kept the revenue that would have gone mainly to high-income homeowners in high-tax states, and the broader tax base was untouched. No constituency for the bill ever formed — not even a single cosponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; the bill died unclaimed

for.name: Sen. Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so its support never took a partisan shape beyond its single Republican sponsor.

industries.note: These households would have received a new federal tax cut worth up to thousands of dollars per year, funded by the broader federal tax base. Because the benefits concentrate at the top of the income scale while the cost spreads across everyone, the industry's interest ran against ordinary taxpayers.

A higher deduction cap makes state and local taxes less burdensome for their residents, easing political resistance to high property and income taxes and making it easier to fund services. The cost lands on the federal government, not the states.
